source.title: More Expressive Feedforward Layers: Part I. Token-Adaptive Mixing of Activations
source.authors: Mingze Wang; Jinbo Wang; Yi-Kuan Xia; Kai Shen; Shu Zhong

record.tranche_reason: The study measures validation-loss scaling across MoE model sizes and fits losses as functions of model size, but uses a different experimental setup and does not report the original studies' power-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The MoE size sweep and its scaling-law panel bear on loss scaling with model size. Other reported results—such as MoA-versus-baseline loss improvements at fixed scales, downstream benchmark scores, and vision convergence—do not test a claim version unless they establish a scaling law or predictability.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper proposing Mixture of Activations (MoA). Its Figure 3 'scaling law' panel fits baseline and MoA loss against model size only to plot the log ratio log(L_baseline/L_method). The point is to show that MoA's gain persists, not to test whether loss follows a power law. No fitted form, exponents or goodness of fit are reported. The 0.25B–2B MoE sweep covers under one order of magnitude, and the curves are not used to extrapolate to larger runs. Nothing tests compute-optimal allocation. Shape is not varied at fixed parameter count. The vision (MAE) experiment compares convergence at one size, and downstream scores come from one size. The scaling-law form is used as a tool to report the method's own advantage, so this is T4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is largely right but incomplete. The authors conclude that MoA (token-adaptive mixing of activation functions) is provably more expressive than learnable or fixed activations at fixed width. Empirically, they find it lowers terminal pre-training loss over tuned baselines in dense (0.12B–0.5B) and MoE (0.25B–2B) LLMs, tolerates larger learning rates, and adds little overhead. They also report gains on 2B downstream benchmarks and MAE vision pre-training. They read the stable gap and near-parallel scaling curves as suggesting gains may persist at larger scale.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares token-adaptive activation-mixing FFNs with standard FFNs in its own training sweeps; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: Model scale, MoA variant, token budget, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and learning-rate tuning vary across experiments. The reported scaling-law panel fits loss as a function of model size, but the fitting form and exponents are not stated.

fits_no_version.finding: Across MoE sizes from 0.25B to 2B (about 0.5–8 PFLOP/s-days), MoA's loss gain over the baseline stays roughly constant. The authors call the one-MoA and baseline curves 'nearly parallel', and the gain exceeds 0.01 in most settings. Figure only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: FFN activation changes shift the loss scaling curve by a roughly constant multiplicative offset without changing its slope.

record.problems: The scaling-law panel provides no numerical fit, exponent, or uncertainty in the supplied text; plotted values are figure-only. The MoE sweep spans 0.25B to 2B parameters and does not test predictions from small runs to much larger runs.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; 10 rows retained, all for the MoE size-scaling results in Figure 3.

untested.parts: All of it. No power-law fit, exponent or fit quality is reported for loss versus parameters, tokens or compute. The MoE sweep spans about 0.25B–2B total parameters.
All of it. No small-run fit is used to predict larger runs.
All of it. No fixed-compute allocation search.
All of it. Depth and width are not varied at fixed parameter count.
All of it. The MAE vision run uses a single model size and compares convergence only.
All of it. Downstream zero-shot scores are reported only for LlamaMoE-2B.
All of it. Fitting choices are not compared.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T2' is wrong. The scaling panel plots only the relative improvement between two fitted curves; the fit form and exponents are never given. All rows are comparisons of the study's own method against its baseline, so their versions are set to none. Dense models use about 20 tokens per parameter (Chinchilla regime) as a design choice, not as a test of V3.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report power-law exponents, test scaling over several orders of magnitude, or establish loss scaling with token count or compute when other factors are not bottlenecks.
No small-run fit is used to predict the loss of substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for loss-minimising parameter and token counts is reported.
The study does not hold parameter count fixed while varying depth, width, or other architecture details to measure their effect on loss.
The vision experiment reports convergence comparisons, not a test of whether the same power-law form holds in vision or another training regime.
Downstream scores are reported for one model size; the study does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not compare fitting choices or establish that exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on setup.
